title: Teotihuacan
para1: Teotihuacan. Teotihuacan was the first great metropolis of the Americas. Founded around 100 BCE in the highlands near today's Mexico City - it began as a religious center of the Mexican Plateau, its great monuments under continuous construction until about 250 CE - it grew until, at its zenith in the first half of the first millennium CE, it was the largest city in the Americas - around 100,000 people, possibly the sixth-largest city in the world at that epoch. It was not an Aztec city: it predated the Aztec Empire by many centuries, and the Aztecs themselves named it, in awe, 'the place where gods were born.' The city was a planned wonder: the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon - among the most architecturally significant pyramids of the pre-Columbian Americas - rose along the great Avenue of the Dead, while the common people lived in multi-floor apartment compounds unique in the ancient Americas; eighty to ninety percent of the valley's population lived in the city, which covered 21 square kilometers and exported obsidian tools across Mesoamerica.
para2: Teotihuacan's influence reached astonishing distances: its presence is documented at sites in Veracruz and deep in the Maya region, where it intervened in the dynastic politics of Maya cities - whether it was the center of a territorial empire is debated; its cultural empire is not. Around 550 CE the city's great monuments were sacked and systematically burned - possibly amid the climate catastrophes of those years - and Teotihuacan slowly emptied. But the later peoples of Mexico never forgot it: the Aztecs claimed common ancestry with its builders and made pilgrimages to its ruins, believing the gods had created the universe there.

title: The Adena & Hopewell Cultures
titleline: The Adena & Hopewell Cultures - The History Web
para1: The Adena and Hopewell Cultures. Long before Europeans arrived, the woodlands of eastern North America were home to mound-building civilizations. The Adena culture came first; then, from 100 BCE to 500 CE, the Hopewell tradition flourished along the rivers of the Northeast and Midwest - not a single society but a widely dispersed set of populations connected by a common network of trade routes, building on the Adena mortuary tradition - the Hopewell Mound Group in Ohio gives the culture its name, and Ohio was its ceremonial heart. The Hopewell exchange system was vast: at its greatest extent it ran from the northern shores of Lake Ontario to the Crystal River mounds of Florida, and along the waterways - the highways of the ancient world - flowed exotic materials from across what is now the United States: obsidian from the Rocky Mountains, copper from the Great Lakes, marine shells from the Gulf Coast, and mica from the southern Appalachians.
para2: The Hopewell peoples converted these raw materials into finished art: their carved steatite platform pipes, among other prestige goods, traveled far and wide and have been found as grave goods in burials far outside the Midwest, and their great earthen mounds and geometric earthworks, raised over their dead, remain among the most impressive monuments of ancient North America. The Hopewell network faded around 500 CE, but the mound-builder tradition it represented did not die: centuries later, the Mississippian culture would raise Cahokia, the greatest city of ancient North America, on the foundations these Woodland cultures laid - an unbroken tradition of monumental mound building that spanned well over a thousand years of the continent's ancient history.

title: The Ancestral Puebloans
titleline: The Ancestral Puebloans - The History Web
para1: The Ancestral Puebloans. The Ancestral Puebloans were the great civilization of the American Southwest - the ancestors of today's Pueblo peoples. They lived across the Colorado Plateau in pit houses, clan houses, grand stone pueblos, and the famous cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde, built into canyon walls for defense; three UNESCO World Heritage Sites - Mesa Verde, Chaco Canyon, and Taos Pueblo - preserve their achievement. Their roots run deep - archaeologists trace the culture's emergence back many thousands of years in the Southwest - and their world was connected by a complex network of roads and communities centered on the great houses of Chaco Canyon; the kiva, the circular ceremonial chamber, was the heart of every community, and their architecture itself encoded a sophisticated knowledge of celestial cycles.
para2: For centuries this civilization flourished in an unforgiving land of mesas and canyons, farming maize where rain was scarce and building their knowledge of the sky into the very alignment of their walls; then, in the 13th century, the great cliff dwellings and canyon cities were abandoned, their people migrating south and east to the pueblos along the Rio Grande where their descendants live today. The older name 'Anasazi' is now avoided: it comes from the Navajo word for 'ancestors of our enemies,' and today's Pueblo peoples consider it derogatory - a reminder that these ruins were never a vanished race's but the homes of a living people's ancestors, whose community at Taos is still inhabited after a thousand years. The cliff dwellings were first brought to wide attention when the rancher Richard Wetherill explored Mesa Verde in 1888-1889, and it was he who applied the Navajo exonym that archaeology later retired.

title: The Classic Maya
titleline: The Classic Maya - The History Web
para1: The Classic Maya. The Classic Maya (c. 250-900 AD) were the most brilliant civilization of the ancient Americas. In the jungles of the Yucatan Peninsula, Guatemala, Belize, and western Honduras - lands where Maya farmers had grown maize, beans, squash, and chili peppers for millennia, built their first cities by 750 BC, and used hieroglyphic writing by the 3rd century BC - dozens of city-states - Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copan - raised sculpted monuments dated by the Long Count calendar, linked by trade, alliance, and war; the two great rivals, Tikal and Calakmul, fought for supremacy for centuries, and even distant Teotihuacan intervened in Maya dynastic politics. Their achievements were intellectual as much as monumental: the Maya script is the most sophisticated writing system of the pre-Columbian Americas, their interlocking ritual calendars and mathematics included one of the earliest explicit uses of zero in human history, and their kings were 'divine kings' thought to mediate between mortals and the supernatural realm, expected to be successful war leaders as well as rulers, though by the Late Classic a growing aristocracy had reduced their once-exclusive power - master artists in jade, obsidian, ceramics, stucco, and painted murals, and practitioners of human sacrifice as part of their religion.
para2: The literate Maya elite recorded their history and ritual knowledge in screenfold books - only three uncontested examples survive - and on countless stelae and ceramics. In the 9th century the central Maya world collapsed into civil wars and abandoned cities, its population shifting north. But the Maya did not vanish: Chichen Itza rose in the Postclassic north, Maya kingdoms still fought the Spanish into the 17th century - the last Maya city fell only in 1697 - and millions of Maya people, speaking Maya languages, live in the same lands today.

title: The Olmec Civilization
titleline: The Olmec Civilization - The History Web
para1: The Olmec Civilization. The Olmecs were the first great civilization of Mesoamerica - often called its 'mother culture.' From roughly 1200 to 400 BC, they flourished in the tropical lowlands of today's Veracruz and Tabasco, on Mexico's Gulf Coast, at a time when most of the Americas knew only villages; they are counted among the cradles of civilization in the Americas. Their first center was San Lorenzo Tenochtitlan; when it declined, they moved to La Venta, with other major sites at Tres Zapotes and Laguna de los Cerros. The Olmecs are famous above all for their colossal heads: massive basalt sculptures, up to several tons each, portraying what are assumed to be individual rulers - the first monumental portraits in the Americas. One head from San Lorenzo stands 1.8 meters tall; a famous seated figure known as 'The Wrestler' shows the same mastery in miniature - Olmec artists were equally at home with six-ton monuments and tiny figurines.
para2: Much of what defines Mesoamerican civilization appears first with the Olmecs: monumental ceremonial centers, the ballgame, long-distance trade in jade and obsidian, and religious imagery that later cultures would inherit. By about 400 BC the great Olmec centers had been abandoned and the population of the eastern heartland dropped precipitously - but elements of their tradition lived on in successor societies, and the pattern they set of cities, kings, gods, and art became the template for every civilization that followed in Mesoamerica, from the Maya to the Aztecs. For centuries afterward the Olmec heartland saw only intermittent occupation, its former glory remembered by the cultures that inherited its gods and its art. They were, in the truest sense, a cradle of American civilization.

title: The Zapotec Civilization
titleline: The Zapotec Civilization - The History Web
para1: The Zapotec Civilization. The Zapotecs - who called themselves Be'ena'a, 'the People who came from the clouds' - built one of the earliest and longest-lived civilizations of Mesoamerica, flourishing in the Valley of Oaxaca from about 700 BC until the Spanish conquest in 1521: more than two thousand years, and archaeological evidence traces their culture back at least 2,500 years. Their capital was Monte Alban, founded around 700 BC on a flattened mountaintop above the valley: one of the first major cities in Mesoamerica, with monumental buildings, ball courts, tombs, and grave goods including finely worked gold jewelry - the whole great plaza carved from the flattened top of a mountain rising over the valley floor. From it, a Zapotec state dominated the territory of today's Oaxaca for a thousand years, until the capital's role passed to Mitla - whose Palace of Columns still stands - and then to Zaachila, which remained the center until the conquest.
para2: The Zapotecs were among the pioneers of Mesoamerican civilization's defining arts: their early monuments carry some of the region's first hieroglyphic writing and calendrical dates - among the oldest texts in the Americas - and their influence reached far beyond Oaxaca in trade, art, and ideas. Remarkably, they survived as a people through every upheaval - the fall of Monte Alban around 700 AD, the rise of the Mixtecs, even the Spanish conquest that ended their state's independence in 1521. The modern Zapotec peoples of Oaxaca - still speaking their ancient language and preserving their distinct identity in the same valleys their ancestors ruled from Monte Alban - are their direct descendants, a remarkable continuity that few civilizations anywhere in the world can match.

title: The Poverty Point Culture
titleline: The Poverty Point Culture - The History Web
para1: The Poverty Point Culture. The Poverty Point culture (c. 1700-1100 BC) built the first great monumental earthworks of North America, centuries before farming transformed the continent. Its center, the site called Poverty Point in northeastern Louisiana, was the hub of a network of hunter-gatherer communities stretching across the lower Mississippi valley and the Gulf coast. There, around 1500 BC, people raised an enormous complex of six concentric earthen ridges, broken by radiating aisles, together with great mounds, including one, known as Mound A, that rises over twenty meters high.
para2: The scale of the work is astonishing. The earthworks at Poverty Point required the movement of hundreds of thousands of cubic meters of soil, carried in basket loads by people who had no agriculture, no pottery tradition to speak of, and no beasts of burden. Yet these were no wandering bands: the site supported a large settled population sustained by the rich fish, game, and wild plants of the bayous, and its workshops produced beads, pendants, and tools on a remarkable scale.
para3: Poverty Point stood at the center of a vast exchange network. Copper from the Great Lakes, galena from Missouri, flint from the Ohio valley, shells from the Gulf, and steatite from the Appalachians all flowed into the site, evidence of trade or gift routes reaching across much of eastern North America. Clay cooking balls, animal figurines, and finely carved beads and effigies are the signatures of the culture at sites across the region.
para4: By about 1100 BC the center faded and the network dissolved, for reasons still debated. Poverty Point was largely forgotten until aerial photography revealed the design of its ridges in the mid-twentieth century. Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage site, recognized as proof that monumental architecture and far-flung exchange in North America began not with farmers or chiefs, but with communities of hunter-gatherers three and a half thousand years ago.

title: The Hohokam and Mogollon Cultures
titleline: The Hohokam and Mogollon Cultures - The History Web
para1: The Hohokam and Mogollon Cultures. The Hohokam and Mogollon cultures (c. AD 200-1450) were two of the great farming traditions of the ancient American Southwest. The Hohokam made their home in the desert basins of southern Arizona, along the Salt and Gila rivers, where they created some of the most extensive irrigation systems of the ancient world: hundreds of miles of canals, dug with stone tools, that watered fields of maize, beans, squash, and cotton in the middle of the desert. Their largest towns, such as Snaketown and later Casa Grande, centered on great houses and ballcourts that show deep ties to the civilizations of Mexico.
para2: The Mogollon, named for the mountain range of New Mexico and Arizona, lived across the rugged uplands to the east. They farmed the mountain valleys, built villages of pithouses and later stone pueblos, and produced one of the glories of ancient American art: Mimbres pottery, bowls painted in black on white with geometric designs and lively figures of animals and people, which were buried with the dead, a hole ritually punched through each base.
para3: Both cultures adapted brilliantly to harsh lands. The Hohokam traded shells from the Gulf of California far into the interior and mastered floodwater farming beside their canals; the Mogollon ranged across deserts, forests, and high valleys, mixing farming with hunting and gathering as the land allowed. At their height, around AD 1000-1300, their towns and fields supported tens of thousands of people.
para4: In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries the great centers were abandoned, as drought, floods that wrecked the canals, and social upheaval reshaped the Southwest. The peoples of the region regrouped into new communities, and the O'odham of the Sonoran Desert are held to be the heirs of the Hohokam. The ruins of Casa Grande and the painted bowls of the Mimbres remain the most eloquent witnesses of these desert civilizations.
source1label: Archaeology Southwest: Archaeological Cultures in the Southwest

title: The Classic Veracruz Culture
titleline: The Classic Veracruz Culture - The History Web
para1: The Classic Veracruz Culture. The Classic Veracruz culture (c. AD 600-1200) flourished along the Gulf coast of Mexico in the centuries after the fall of Teotihuacan. Its people built ceremonial cities dominated by stepped pyramids, palaces, and ballcourts, the greatest of them El Tajin, near the modern city of Papantla. At its height El Tajin was one of the largest cities in Mesoamerica, its plazas framed by pyramids decorated with recessed niches, carved panels, and flying cornices, the most famous being the Pyramid of the Niches, whose 365 niches are often linked to the solar year.
para2: The culture is renowned above all for its art of the ballgame. The ritual ballgame, played with a heavy rubber ball, had deep religious meaning across Mesoamerica, and Veracruz artists carved its equipment and its mythology in extraordinary detail: the famous palmas, yokes, and hachas, ornate stone objects worn or displayed in connection with the game, show players, deities, and scenes of sacrifice. El Tajin alone has more than a dozen ballcourts, and its carved panels depict the ritual death that followed the sacred game.
para3: Classic Veracruz society was a world of rival city-states sharing a common elite culture. Its rulers traded and warred along the coast, its sculptors worked in a distinctive style of interlaced scrolls and figures, and its influence reached deep into the Mexican highlands and toward the Maya region. Scholars still debate the ethnicity of its people, who may have been ancestors of the Totonacs of the region today.
para4: The culture declined around 1200 as new powers rose in central Mexico, and El Tajin was abandoned to the forest, its ruins hidden until the eighteenth century. Rediscovered and excavated, it is now a UNESCO World Heritage site, and its pyramids and ballcourt carvings stand among the masterpieces of ancient Mexico.
source2label: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: El Tajin, Pre-Hispanic City

title: The Dorset Culture
titleline: The Dorset Culture - The History Web
para1: Long before the ancestors of today's Inuit spread across the Arctic, a different people made the far north their home. Archaeologists call them the Dorset, after Cape Dorset on Baffin Island where their remains were first recognized; Inuit oral tradition remembers them as the Tuniit. Growing out of the earlier Pre-Dorset tradition around 500 BCE, Dorset people occupied the coasts of Arctic Canada, Labrador, and Greenland for some fifteen centuries. They were master cold-country hunters who lived in small, mobile bands, taking seals at their breathing holes through the winter ice, hunting caribou and muskox on land, and lighting their snow houses and sod-walled dwellings with soapstone lamps burning seal oil.
para2: Dorset life left few grand monuments, but it produced one of the most striking small-scale art traditions in the ancient Americas. Dorset carvers shaped walrus ivory, antler, bone, and driftwood into miniature bears, seals, falcons, human figures, and masks, many of them probably used in hunting rituals or shamanic practice. The famous 'swimming bears', only a few centimetres long, show bears gliding through water with an ease that speaks to long observation of Arctic animals. Unlike their successors, the Dorset apparently made little or no use of dogsleds, large skin boats, or the bow and arrow, which shaped both their hunting style and their vulnerability.
para3: Dorset fortunes turned with the climate. After about 1000 CE a warming period shifted sea-ice patterns and game routes, and at the same time the Thule people, ancestors of the modern Inuit, moved rapidly eastward from Alaska with dog teams, large boats, and whale-hunting gear. Dorset communities disappeared as Thule settlements spread; the nature and extent of contact remain debated. The Sadlermiut of Southampton Island, who survived until disease carried by whalers destroyed them in 1902-03, were long thought to be the last Dorset; modern genetic study has shown they were in fact of Thule, not Dorset, descent.
para4: The Dorset were recognized as a distinct culture only in 1925, when archaeologist Diamond Jenness separated their strange artifacts from those of other Arctic peoples. Genetic studies have since confirmed that they were a separate population, largely replaced rather than absorbed by the Thule. Their tiny carvings, now held in museums across the world, remain the most eloquent testimony to a hardy people who thrived for longer than a millennium in one of Earth's harshest environments.
description: The Dorset culture (Tuniit): the Paleo-Inuit people of the Canadian Arctic and Greenland, their ivory art, and their disappearance after the Thule expansion.

article.p: Long before the ancestors of today's Inuit spread across the Arctic, a different people made the far north their home. Archaeologists call them the Dorset, after Cape Dorset - Kinngait - on Baffin Island, where their remains were first recognized; Inuit oral tradition remembers them as the Tuniit, a race of strong giants who came before. Growing out of the earlier Pre-Dorset tradition around 800 to 500 BCE, Dorset people occupied the coasts of Arctic Canada and Greenland for some two thousand years, one of the longest-enduring cultures of the ancient Americas.

The Dorset were marine hunters of remarkable skill. They took seals and walrus at the breathing holes and ice edges with heavy harpoons, drove caribou along stone fences inland, and fished and fowled in season - yet they never used the bow and arrow, and unlike the Inuit who followed them they did not hunt the great whales. They pulled hand sleds, cut snow blocks with snow knives for winter houses, and lit and warmed their homes with carved soapstone lamps. In the Late Dorset period they even cold-hammered metal - copper gathered from the Coppermine River and iron pried from the Cape York meteorite in Greenland - and a few objects of smelted metal hint at encounters with the Norse then settling in southern Greenland.

Dorset life left few grand monuments, but it produced one of the most striking small-scale art traditions in the ancient Americas. Dorset carvers shaped walrus ivory, antler, bone, and driftwood into miniature bears, seals, falcons, human figures, and masks, many of them probably used in hunting ritual or by spiritual specialists. The famous swimming bears, only a few centimeters long, show bears gliding through the water with an economy of line that modern artists envy. At Qajartalik in Nunavik they carved faces into the bedrock itself - the only known rock art of the eastern Arctic from this age.

figure.cap: A Dorset swimming bear in walrus ivory, a few centimeters long - the most famous product of the Dorset carvers' art. Musee du quai Branly, photo CC BY 2.0.

figure.alt: Dorset ivory carving of a sea mammal
figure.cap: A sea mammal carved in ivory - the seal was the Dorset hunter's staff of life, giving food, fuel, clothing, and raw material. Musee du quai Branly, photo CC BY 2.0.

article.p: Dorset fortunes turned near the end of the first millennium. The climate shifted, sea-ice patterns and game routes moved, and after about 1000 CE the Thule people - ancestors of the modern Inuit - swept rapidly eastward from Alaska with dog teams, large skin boats, and whale-hunting gear. Dorset communities vanished as Thule settlements spread; how the two peoples met, and how much contact, conflict, or disease passed between them, is still debated. On Southampton Island the Sadlermiut, whose ancestry and culture long puzzled scholars, kept a Dorset-derived way of life into recent centuries before an introduced epidemic destroyed them in 1902-1903.

The Dorset were recognized as a distinct culture only in 1925, when the archaeologist Diamond Jenness separated their strange artifacts from those of other Arctic peoples and named the culture for Cape Dorset. Genetic studies have since confirmed that they were a separate population, largely replaced rather than absorbed by the Thule. Their tiny carvings, now held in museums across the world, remain the most eloquent testimony of a hardy people who made the Arctic their own for two thousand years.

title: Archaic North America and the Shift to Settled Communities
titleline: Archaic North America and the Shift to Settled Communities - The History Web
imagealt: Monks Mound at the Cahokia site, 1882 engraving (a much later Mississippian site)
para1: Archaic cultures were ancient cultures of North and South America that developed from Paleo-Indian traditions and led to the adoption of agriculture. Britannica says they are defined by shared characteristics rather than a particular date or place. Their Paleo-Indian predecessors were highly nomadic, specialized hunters and gatherers. Archaic peoples lived in larger groups, stayed in one place for part of the year, and ate a highly varied diet. In the Southwest, the National Park Service dates the Archaic from the end of the Paleoindian period, with the earliest dates around 8,500 BC, to the adoption of agriculture in the north and pottery in the south, as late as the first few centuries AD in some places.
para2: Archaic peoples were generalists. Their food remains include rabbits, antelope, deer, elk, moose and bison, water birds and land birds, fish and shellfish, and plant foods such as tubers, roots, seeds, fruits and nuts, chosen according to the season. They made tools not seen before in the Americas. Basketry and netting helped collect and store new plant foods, and grinding stones, including manos and metates, made hard seeds edible. Hunting kit included tanged and side-notched projectile points, atlatl weights, nets for birds and small game, and fishhooks. Britannica suggests that new foods and new tools probably developed together.
para3: A more reliable food supply let larger groups gather, and people became more settled and more socially complex. In the late Archaic, people began to tend plants to a limited degree. East of the Mississippi River they focused on pigweed and related species, while groups in Mesoamerica worked with wild maize. Even then they depended mostly on hunting and gathering. The National Park Service divides the Southwest Archaic into Early (8,500 to 4,000 BC), Middle (4,000 to 2,000 BC) and Late (2,000 BC to as late as AD 500) phases, and notes a large increase in human presence and in settled life in the Late Archaic, tied to growing use of plant foods.
para4: When a population puts more weight on producing food, Britannica says it is generally classed as a Woodland culture in the Eastern Woodlands, Southeast and Plains, or as an early Puebloan culture in the Southwest. The National Park Service reports farming in the Southwest as early as 2,000 BC and irrigation by 1,000 BC even in the north. The picture on this page is an 1882 engraving of Monks Mound at Cahokia. It belongs to a much later society. OpenStax describes Cahokia at its height, about AD 1100, as a city of more than ten thousand people with about 120 earthen mounds, which declined after AD 1300. It is shown here as a later example of mound building, not as an Archaic site.
source2label: National Park Service: The Archaic Period
